Gaza flotilla issues mayday as drones and vessels harass aid ship

A vessel from the Gaza flotilla mission, the Adalah, has issued a mayday call to the Greek coast guard reporting drones and unidentified vessels harassing its humanitarian mission in international waters.

Activists on board say they are being surveilled and intimidated as they continue toward Gaza.

The distress call comes just days after Israeli forces illegally intercepted a major flotilla of over 50 vessels near Crete, detaining around 175 activists in international waters.

Many were transferred to Greece, where dozens required medical treatment, and many reported mistreatment.

Two activists, Saif Abu Keshek and Thiago Avila, were separated from the others and taken to Israel, where they remain detained.

Both have reported mistreatment, including being bound, blindfolded and assaulted, with governments including Spain and Brazil condemning their illegal detention.

Israel court extends detention of two Gaza flotilla activists

An Israeli court Sunday extended by two days the detention of two activists from a Gaza-bound flotilla, who were brought to Israel for questioning.

Spanish national Saif Abu Keshek and Brazilian Thiago Avila appeared before a court in the southern city of Ashkelon on Sunday.

They were taken by Israeli forces to Israel on Thursday after their vessel was illegally intercepted along with 50 other boats in international waters off the coast of Greece, more than 1,000 kilometres away from Gaza.

The two activists reported being treated with "extreme brutality” by Israeli forces.

Filmmaker Akinola Davies Jr concluded his acceptance speech at the BAFTAs with a call for “a free Palestine,” but the line was removed from the televised broadcast on the BBC.

Davies Jr who was being recognised by the British Academy of Film and Television Arts for work exploring Black British life and diasporic identity, made the remark while thanking collaborators and reflecting on global injustices. When the ceremony aired, viewers noticed the reference to the State of Palestine had been cut.

 The edit prompted criticism of the BBC for censoring a political statement and curbing free expression during a major cultural event.
